doc.title: Virginia Mayhew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 23, 2022

chapter: Working with Al Grey and Diva
title: Sexism and women instrumentalists
summary: Mayhew attributes resistance to women playing saxophone to sexism and societal norms, wartime work, and difficulty combining family with a jazz life.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You made a comment in an article that even though you were told that — no play the clarinet instead, girls don’t play the saxophone, that it’s better now.
What’s the main reason you think that there’s been such resistance going back decades, for women to play certain instruments?

I mean sexism basically, and you know societal norms of what women can and can’t do. Apparently during World War II when all the guys went over to fight, women stepped up and did all those gigs and then I don’t know where they came from, they must have already existed. They didn’t start from scratch. But then when they came back all the work stopped again. So I think it’s a cultural thing and also with wanting to have a family. Or are you talking about elementary school?
No, no, I’m talking about the professional world.

Yeah. Wanting to have a family doesn’t — it’s a lot better now — people seem to be able to pull it off more, but it’s really hard to live that kind of a lifestyle if you want a family with kids, especially when you’re young. My friend Ingrid Jensen, who is very successful, she didn’t have her child until she was in her 40s and already well established. I just can’t imagine how anybody could have a child early unless you have like somebody that’s going to stay home and take care of the kid and have a career when you need to be out, in your formative years and stuff like that. Did I get off topic there?
